That the horns and the tiger skin come from a direction on the compass. And that oni are the ones who get chased away. One by one, we will hold each of them up against the old sources.

segments.text: The chronicle tells of the year six sixty-one. Empress Saimei had moved her court to a temporary palace in Kyushu, in the west of Japan. That summer, she died there. Then, after the crown prince had brought her remains back to the Palace of Ihase, that evening, on the top of Mount Asakura, there was an oni. It wore a large hat, and it looked down on the funeral. Everyone who saw it cried out in wonder. When W. G. Aston translated this passage into English in eighteen ninety-six, he wrote demon, and added a note: or spirit. The chronicle says nothing about horns, tiger skin, or a club.

segments.text: About seventy years after these events, in seven thirty-three, the province of Izumo completed a record of its land, the Izumo Fudoki. It explains the name of one village, Ayo, with a story. Long ago, a man was farming a mountain field. A one-eyed oni came and ate his son. The parents hid in a bamboo thicket, and the bamboo leaves stirred. As he was being eaten, the son cried out, ayo, ayo. And so the place was called Ayo.

segments.text: The third claim explains the horns and the tiger skin. In seventeen seventy-nine, the artist Toriyama Sekien published a book of monsters. Beside his oni, he wrote a short note. People call the northeast, the direction of the ox and the tiger, the demon gate. When oni are painted today, they wear the horns of an ox on their heads and the skin of a tiger around their waists. This shape, he says, is said to join the ox and the tiger together.
